title: Sahih Muslim
hook: Muslim's Sahih, known for its careful arrangement

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sahih al-Bukhari, the sound collection, which opens with a hadith on intentions.

A desk, a lamp, and a stack of notes. One saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has reached you along several chains of narrators, each wording it a little differently. One adds a detail. One gives the whole scene; another, only the saying. So where do they go in your book? Scattered, a piece here and a piece there, wherever each fits a topic? Or all together, side by side, so a reader can see every version and spot exactly where they differ? One scholar chose the second way, and it's what his book is known for. Today, Sahih Muslim.
screen: `ONE SAYING, SEVERAL CHAINS.` → `SCATTER THEM, OR GATHER THEM?` → `SAHIH MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, from the city of Nishapur. Muslim here is his name, not only his faith. Tradition says he studied with al-Bukhari and held him in deep respect. Two students of one science, two books with the same name, sahih, sound. Together they're called the two Sahihs. Second, the arrangement. Al-Bukhari sometimes divided a hadith across his book, a piece under each heading where it proved a point. Muslim, for the most part, kept a hadith in one place and laid its chains and wordings next to each other. For a student, that's a gift: you can watch one saying travel down several roads and see the exact place where a word changes. Third, the doorway. Before the hadith begin, Muslim wrote an introduction. In it he explains why he takes reports only from people known to be reliable, and he warns against passing things on carelessly. He records a saying of the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak: the chain of narrators is part of the religion, and without it, anyone could say whatever they liked. Everything from last week, in one line. Fourth, one hadith from inside. In Muslim's book, the Prophet says that Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but looks at your hearts and your deeds. Hearts and deeds, together. Scholars have weighed the two Sahihs against each other, and not all of them came down on the same side. This path takes them as a pair.
screen: `MUSLIM IBN AL-HAJJAJ, OF NISHAPUR.` · `EVERY CHAIN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE CHAIN IS PART OF THE RELIGION.` · `HEARTS AND DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Let today's hadith land: Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but at your hearts and your deeds. Recall the last time you sized someone up by how they looked, the clothes, the face, the car, then turn it around: what did you spend on your appearance this week, and what on your heart? No verdict, just look, the way you'd look at a receipt; if you pray, you can carry this hadith into your next prayer.
Sahih Muslim. The second of the two Sahihs, where each hadith's chains and wordings are gathered in one place, side by side. Today's word.
Your line: the second sahih. What Allah looks at: hearts and deeds, not faces. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sunni Muslims study Sahih Muslim alongside Sahih al-Bukhari, and teachers often use its gathered chains to show students how one hadith came down in several wordings.

notes: Ibn al-Mubarak's saying ('the isnad is part of the religion; were it not for the isnad, whoever wished would say whatever he wished') as recorded in the Muqaddimah of Sahih Muslim: confirm placement.
Muslim 2564 (Allah does not look at your bodies/forms but at your hearts and deeds): confirm number; some versions read 'bodies and forms', paraphrased here as 'bodies or faces'.
Tradition that Muslim studied with al-Bukhari: framed as tradition; confirm.
Description of Bukhari dividing hadith across chapters and Muslim gathering chains in one place: a general characterization; confirm it is fair.

'Scholars have weighed the two Sahihs against each other ... not all came down on the same side': refers to the classical debate (some Maghribi scholars preferring Muslim); kept vague under the claims rule. Confirm.
Ibn al-Mubarak's saying was also used on day 1060 (year 3); here it is tied to Muslim's introduction specifically. Cut if too close.
